title: Agents, Access, and the Future of Machine Identity — Nick Nisi (WorkOS) + Lizzie Siegle (Cloudflare)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central thesis is machine identity, OAuth for agents, and fine-grained authorization, directly matching security_safety_identity_governance inclusion criteria for identity and authorization of AI systems. Cloudflare Workers and WorkOS are developer platforms for building secure agent infrastructure, while the identity and authorization concepts apply across application verticals. The talk demonstrates development and deployment of an MCP server with OAuth integration via Wrangler, plus production-readiness warnings about the OAuth-less template. Requires familiarity with OAuth flows, MCP, and Cloudflare platform concepts but remains accessible through demo-driven explanations. Recorded conference talk at AI Engineer World's Fair featuring live demonstrations of MCP server deployment and agent authorization. summary: Lizzie Siegle (Cloudflare developer advocate) and Nick Nisi (WorkOS developer experience engineer) explore how machine identity must evolve as AI agents act on behalf of users. Lizzie opens by describing agents she built—auto-voting in NBA finals, booking tennis courts—and raises the core question: how do you control what agents are allowed to do? Nick frames the problem: MCP servers currently require editing JSON and providing personal access tokens, which is too advanced for non-developers. WorkOS handles authorization and user management, and the talk's thesis is that agents need the same OAuth-based credentials and authorization as user-facing applications. Lizzie highlights Cloudflare's broader platform: Workers (edge compute), vectorized (vector database), SQL database, Durable Objects (per-user persistent storage used in their agents framework), KV storage, and bindings to connect Cloudflare products. Durable Objects now have a free tier. They demo an MCP server deployed via Wrangler, connected to Claude as a client. Through OAuth sign-in (GitHub), Claude authenticates on behalf of the user and can order a shirt, list inventory, retrieve user info from JWT claims (including roles/permissions and a custom 'favorite song' claim), and store order data in Cloudflare KV. Durable Objects maintain per-user context, demonstrated by toggling a 'demo mode' to 'banned'—which blocks further shirt orders until a 'pretty please' tool overrides it. They envision future fine-grained authorization (per-line changes, per-tool, per-network) and emphasize audit trails. Users should be thought of as deputies with tools they can use or misuse. A click-to-deploy template exists but is OAuth-less (not recommended for production); an OAuth-enabled version is slightly slower but secure.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: OAuth is no longer just for humans—agents acting on behalf of users need proper authentication and authorization credentials.
MCP servers currently require manual JSON editing and personal access tokens, which is too advanced for non-developer end users.
Cloudflare's platform (Workers, Durable Objects, KV, bindings) provides building blocks for agent infrastructure with per-user state and persistence.
Durable Objects enable per-user storage close to the user, now available on a free tier.
JWT claims can carry user identity, roles, permissions, and custom data that agents use to personalize and authorize actions.
Fine-grained authorization (per-tool, per-action, per-network) and audit trails are the future direction for agent access control.
Users should be conceptualized as deputies who can both use and misuse the tools delegated to them.
An OAuth-less click-to-deploy MCP template exists for speed but should not be used in production.
The demo MCP server and repo are available; mcp.shop lets anyone run the same shirt-ordering workflow.
Understand why traditional OAuth and session tokens need extension for agent-based access

sections.title: Introduction and the Problem of Agent Access Control
sections.summary: Lizzie and Nick introduce themselves. Lizzie describes building agents that act on her behalf (NBA voting, tennis court booking). Nick explains that MCP servers require manual JSON editing and PATs, which is too advanced for non-developers. The thesis emerges: agents need the same OAuth-based credentials as user-facing apps.

sections.title: Cloudflare Platform Overview for Agent Infrastructure
sections.summary: Lizzie challenges assumptions about Cloudflare, listing Workers, vectorized, SQL database, Durable Objects for agent memory, and bindings. Durable Objects now have a free tier. The agents framework uses Durable Objects for persistence and includes an OAuth framework for identifying who an agent acts on behalf of.

sections.title: Live Demo: Deploying and Connecting the MCP Server
sections.summary: They deploy an MCP server via `npm run deploy` (Wrangler), copy the Workers URL, and add it as an integration in Claude named 'MCP Shop.' OAuth sign-in with GitHub authenticates the agent on behalf of the user, making tools available.

sections.title: Live Demo: Ordering a Shirt and Viewing Stored Data
sections.summary: Claude lists inventory, orders a free MCP shirt (XL, WorkOS, Bellevue Nebraska), and returns an order number. The order data is visible in Cloudflare KV storage. A get-user-info tool reveals JWT claims including name, email, favorite song, and admin permissions.

sections.title: Durable Objects and Per-User State with Demo Mode
sections.summary: Nick explains Durable Objects as per-user, fast storage on the worker context. Lizzie toggles demo mode to 'banned,' which blocks further shirt orders. A 'pretty please' tool overrides the ban, demonstrating per-user stored state and permission-based tool access.

sections.title: Future Directions and Call to Action
sections.summary: They envision fine-grained authorization (per-line, per-tool, per-network) and audit trails. A click-to-deploy OAuth-less template exists for speed. Users are framed as deputies who can misuse tools. The repo and mcp.shop are shared for the audience to try.

demonstrations: Deploying an MCP server to Cloudflare via `npm run deploy` using Wrangler, receiving a Workers URL
Connecting the deployed MCP server to Claude client as an integration called 'MCP Shop'
OAuth sign-in with GitHub through WorkOS to authenticate the agent on behalf of the user
Ordering a shirt through Claude by providing size, company name, and mailing address, receiving an order number
Viewing order data stored in Cloudflare KV storage via the Cloudflare dashboard
Retrieving user info from JWT claims including name, email, favorite song, and admin permissions
Toggling demo mode to 'banned' via a tool stored on the Durable Object, blocking further shirt orders
Using a 'pretty please' tool to override the ban and order another shirt, demonstrating per-user stored state
limitations: OAuth-less click-to-deploy template is fast but not recommended for production use
MCP server configuration requires editing JSON files, which is too advanced for non-developers
mcp.shop does not include the 'pretty please' tool
Live demo depends on Wi-Fi reliability
GitHub MCP and similar tools are developer-centric
quantitativeClaims: Durable Objects now have a free tier (previously not free)
Startups exist that use Cloudflare without paying and still make money
